title: Part III: Colonialism and the Countryside: Exploring Official Archives

topics.title: Colonialism in the countryside and official archives

learn.hook: Revenue records, surveys and commission reports were written to serve the Company. Today historians read them to recover the stories of zamindars, tribal peoples and peasants.
points: Colonial rule affected rural society deeply, mainly through new land revenue policies, changes in property rights and the expansion of markets.

This chapter looks at three regions: Bengal and its zamindars under the Permanent Settlement; the Rajmahal hills (in present-day Jharkhand), home of the Paharias and Santhals; and the Bombay Deccan (western Maharashtra), where ryots revolted against moneylenders.

Historians use official sources: revenue records, survey reports, reports of commissions and committees, and travelogues by officials. These were produced by the colonial state for its own purposes: to collect revenue, control territory and justify policy.
Because they reflect official concerns, historians read them critically, asking who wrote them, why, and what they left out, and comparing them with other evidence.
Map work: Bengal (Burdwan), the Rajmahal hills and the Santhal Pargana (Jharkhand), and the Bombay Deccan (Poona and Ahmednagar).

topics.title: An auction in Burdwan and the Permanent Settlement

learn.hook: In 1797, estates of the Raja of Burdwan were auctioned for unpaid revenue. Many 'buyers' turned out to be the Raja's own agents!
points: In 1797 an auction was held in Burdwan (present-day Bardhaman). Several mahals (estates) held by the Raja of Burdwan were sold because he had accumulated huge arrears of revenue.

Many of the purchasers were the Raja's own servants and agents who bought the lands on his behalf. These were benami purchases (literally 'anonymous'), made in the name of an insignificant person while the real beneficiary stayed hidden. In this way the Raja kept control of his estates.

The auctions were a result of the Permanent Settlement introduced in Bengal in 1793 by the East India Company under Governor-General Lord Cornwallis. The revenue each zamindar had to pay was fixed permanently, and estates of those who failed to pay were auctioned.

The Company saw rajas and taluqdars as zamindars. A zamindar was not a landowner in the village but a revenue collector of the state; a zamindari could include as many as 400 villages. Zamindars collected rent from ryots and paid fixed revenue to the Company.

Aims: Bengal's economy was in crisis, with recurrent famines and falling output. Officials hoped that fixing revenue permanently would ensure a regular flow of revenue to the Company, encourage investment in land (since landholders would keep any increased profits), and create a class of loyal landholders and 'improving' farmers with capital and enterprise.

example.answer: Through benami purchases by his agents, so the estates stayed under his control.

learn.hook: If the revenue did not reach the treasury by sunset on the due date, the zamindari could be auctioned. That was the 'Sunset Law'!
points: Revenue arrears were common, and many zamindaris were auctioned in the decades after the Permanent Settlement. Several reasons explain this.

First, the initial demand was very high. Since the demand was fixed for all time, the Company feared it could never claim a share of increased income later, so it pegged the demand high, arguing the burden would fall as production expanded and prices rose.

Second, this high demand was imposed in the 1790s, when prices of agricultural produce were depressed, making it hard for ryots to pay their dues to the zamindar. Third, the revenue was invariable, regardless of the harvest, and had to be paid punctually; under the Sunset Law, if payment did not come in by sunset of the specified date, the zamindari could be auctioned.

Fourth, the Settlement initially limited the zamindar's power to collect rent and manage the zamindari. Zamindars' troops were disbanded, customs duties abolished, and their cutcheries (courts) brought under the supervision of a Collector appointed by the Company. They lost the power to organise local justice and police; the collectorate became an alternative centre of authority.
Fifth, ryots sometimes delayed payment deliberately, encouraged by rich peasants, and harvests were uneven. Zamindars could take defaulting ryots to court, but justice was slow.

example.answer: Because of high fixed demand, low prices, the rigid Sunset Law, reduced zamindari powers and ryots' resistance.

learn.hook: While zamindars struggled, a group of rich peasants in the villages of north Bengal grew so powerful that they could defy zamindars and even buy their estates!
points: By the end of the eighteenth century, rich peasants were consolidating their position in villages. In parts of Bengal they were called jotedars; elsewhere haoladars, gantidars or mandals. Francis Buchanan's survey of Dinajpur district vividly describes the jotedars.

By the early nineteenth century, jotedars had acquired vast areas of land, sometimes several thousand acres. They controlled local trade and moneylending, exercising immense power over poorer cultivators.
Much of their land was cultivated by sharecroppers (adhiyars or bargadars), who brought their own ploughs, worked the fields and handed over half the produce to the jotedar after the harvest.

Unlike zamindars, who often lived in towns, jotedars lived in the villages, so their power within villages was more effective. They fiercely resisted zamindars' efforts to increase the jama (revenue) of the village, prevented zamindari officials from doing their work, mobilised dependent ryots and deliberately delayed revenue payments.
When zamindars' estates were auctioned for arrears, jotedars were often among the purchasers. They were most powerful in north Bengal.

topics.title: Zamindars resist, and the Fifth Report

learn.hook: Over 800 of the Fifth Report's 1,002 pages were appendices: petitions, collectors' reports and tables. It was a monster of a document, and it had an agenda!
points: Zamindars found ways to survive. The Raja of Burdwan first transferred part of his zamindari to his mother, since the Company had decreed that the property of women would not be taken over.

At auctions, zamindars' agents manipulated the proceedings: they outbid genuine buyers and then refused to pay, so the estate had to be resold; this was repeated until the price fell and the zamindar's agent bought it cheaply. Through such fictitious sales and benami purchases, zamindars kept control. Lathyals (lathi-wielding strongmen) sometimes drove off outside buyers, and ryots also resisted outsiders.
By the early nineteenth century the depression in prices ended. Zamindars who had survived the 1790s consolidated their power, and the Company relaxed its rules of revenue payment.

The Fifth Report, submitted to the British Parliament in 1813, was the fifth of a series of reports on the administration and activities of the East India Company in India. It ran to 1,002 pages, of which over 800 were appendices reproducing petitions of zamindars and ryots, reports of collectors, statistical tables and notes on revenue and judicial administration of Bengal and Madras.

In Britain, many groups attacked the Company's monopoly and its officials' corruption, and Parliament passed Acts to regulate Company rule and demanded regular reports. The Fifth Report became the basis of intense debates. Historians note it exaggerated the collapse of traditional zamindari power and the scale on which zamindars were losing land.

topics.title: The hoe: Buchanan and the Paharias

learn.hook: Plains zamindars paid tribute to hill chiefs to stop raids, and traders paid tolls to use mountain passes. The Paharias were masters of their hills!
points: Francis Buchanan was a physician in the Bengal Medical Service who undertook detailed surveys for the East India Company. In 1810–11 he travelled through the Rajmahal hills. He looked at the landscape as a Company employee, judging its potential for 'improvement' and commercial value.

The Paharias lived around the Rajmahal hills. They subsisted on forest produce and practised shifting cultivation: they cleared patches by cutting bushes and burning undergrowth, which enriched the soil with potash, and grew pulses and millets, scratching the ground lightly with hoes. After a few years they left the land fallow.

They collected mahua flowers for food, silk cocoons and resin for sale, and wood for charcoal. Their identity was intimately linked with the forest. Their chiefs maintained unity, settled disputes and led the tribe in battles.

The Paharias regularly raided the plains where settled farmers lived. Raids helped them survive in years of scarcity, asserted their power over settled communities, and were a way of negotiating political relations with outsiders.

Plains zamindars purchased peace by paying regular tribute to hill chiefs. Traders paid a small amount for permission to use passes controlled by them; once paid, Paharia chiefs protected the traders' goods.

example.q: How did the Paharias respond to outsiders before the late eighteenth century?

So they negotiated power with outsiders on their own terms.

topics.title: The plough: pacification, Santhals and Damin-i-Koh

learn.hook: From 40 Santhal villages in 1838 to 1,473 by 1851: the Damin-i-Koh filled with plough farmers, and the Paharias were pushed deeper into the hills.
points: In the last decades of the eighteenth century, settled agriculture expanded aggressively in eastern India. To the British, extending settled agriculture would enlarge land revenue, produce crops for export and create a settled, ordered society. They saw forest people as savage, unruly and difficult to govern.

In the 1770s the British followed a brutal policy of extermination, hunting down and killing Paharias. By the 1780s, Augustus Cleveland, the Collector of Bhagalpur, proposed pacification: Paharia chiefs were given an annual allowance and made responsible for their men's conduct. Many refused; those who accepted lost authority in their community as stipendaries of the government. Many Paharias withdrew deep into the mountains.

Around 1800 the Santhals began coming into the area. They cleared forests, cut timber, ploughed the land and grew rice and cotton. The British saw them as ideal settlers: hardworking and good at reclaiming land. Zamindars also hired them to expand cultivation.

In 1832 a large area was demarcated as the Damin-i-Koh, declared the land of the Santhals. They were to live within it and practise plough agriculture. The land grant required that at least one-tenth of the area be cleared and cultivated within the first ten years. The area was surveyed, mapped and enclosed by boundary pillars.

Santhal settlements grew rapidly: from 40 villages in 1838 to 1,473 villages by 1851, and the population rose from about 3,000 to over 82,000. As Santhals occupied the lower hills, the Paharias had to recede further. This was a conflict between the hoe, symbol of shifting cultivation, and the plough, symbol of settled agriculture.

As Santhals expanded, Paharias lost land and moved deeper into the hills.
example.answer: Because the plough-using Santhals, backed by the British, expanded at the expense of the hoe-using Paharias.

learn.reallife: The Santhal Pargana division of Jharkhand, with towns like Dumka and Sahibganj, grew out of the Damin-i-Koh area.

topics.title: The Santhal rebellion and Buchanan's account as a source

learn.hook: The Santhals cleared forests to farm, but soon found their land slipping away to taxes, moneylenders and zamindars. In 1855 they rose in revolt, the hul!
points: The Santhals soon found that the land they had brought under cultivation was slipping away. The state levied heavy taxes; moneylenders (dikus) charged high rates of interest and took over land when debts were unpaid; and zamindars asserted control over the Damin area.

By the 1850s the Santhals felt the time had come to rebel against zamindars, moneylenders and the colonial state, to create an ideal world where they would rule themselves. The Santhal rebellion (hul) of 1855–56 was led by figures such as Sidhu and Kanhu.

After the revolt, the Santhal Pargana was created, carved out of the districts of Bhagalpur and Birbhum (about 5,500 square miles). The colonial state hoped that a new territory with some special laws would conciliate the Santhals.
Buchanan's account is a valuable source: it describes landscapes, crops, settlements, forest products and peoples in rich detail.

But it also has limits. Buchanan wrote as a Company employee, interested in resources and 'improvement'; he was critical of forest dwellers' ways of life and saw forests as land to be turned into fields. His account reveals what the Company valued, and conceals how local people themselves saw their world.

topics.title: Account books come to be burnt: Supa, 1875

learn.hook: On 12 May 1875, ryots in Supa village near Poona demanded the moneylenders' account books and set them on fire. Paper had become a symbol of oppression!
points: On 12 May 1875, ryots from surrounding rural areas gathered at Supa, a large village in Poona district (present-day Maharashtra), where many shopkeepers and moneylenders lived.

They attacked the shopkeepers and moneylenders (sahukars), demanding their bahi khatas (account books) and debt bonds. They burnt the khatas, looted grain shops and in some cases set fire to sahukars' houses.

From Poona the revolt spread to Ahmednagar, and over the next two months to many more villages. Everywhere the pattern was similar: sahukars were attacked, account books burnt and debt bonds destroyed.
Terrified sahukars fled their villages, often leaving their property behind. British police posts were set up in villages, and many people were arrested and convicted.
The ryots' anger focused on the account books and bonds because these records were the instruments through which they believed they had been cheated and trapped in debt.

topics.title: Ryotwari, Ricardo and the debt trap

learn.hook: In the Bombay Deccan, the Company dealt directly with each ryot and resurveyed lands every 30 years. Sounds fair? Not when the demand was too high!
points: After the Bengal experience, a different system was introduced in the Bombay Deccan in the 1820s: the ryotwari settlement, made directly with the ryot. The average income from different types of soil was estimated, the ryot's revenue-paying capacity assessed and a proportion fixed as the state's share. Lands were resurveyed every 30 years and revenue rates increased. The demand was not permanent.

Officials were influenced by the economist David Ricardo, who argued that a landowner should have a claim only to the 'average rent' prevailing at a given time. When land yielded more than this, the surplus should be taxed by the state; otherwise cultivators would become rentiers and not invest productively. Many officials thought Bengal's ryots had turned into rentiers, confirming Ricardo's theory.

The first revenue settlement in the Bombay Deccan was so high that in many places peasants deserted their villages and migrated to new regions, especially in areas of poor soil and fluctuating rainfall. When rains failed and harvests were poor, peasants could not pay; collectors, keen to show efficiency, seized property and imposed fines.
In the 1830s, agricultural prices fell sharply and did not recover for about fifteen years, cutting peasants' incomes further. Famine also struck the countryside.

To pay revenue and meet everyday and production needs, ryots borrowed from moneylenders. Once taken, loans were hard to repay; as debts mounted, ryots became dependent on moneylenders. By the 1840s officials found alarming levels of peasant indebtedness everywhere.

example.q: How did a Deccan ryot fall into a debt trap?

Prices fell in the 1830s, reducing income.

So he became dependent on the moneylender.
example.answer: High revenue and falling prices forced borrowing; mounting interest made repayment impossible, trapping him in debt.

learn.hook: When the American Civil War broke out in 1861, cotton from India suddenly became gold. Then the war ended, and the boom collapsed!
points: Before the 1860s, three-fourths of the raw cotton imports into Britain came from America. British cotton manufacturers, worried about this dependence, formed bodies like the Cotton Supply Association (1857) and the Manchester Cotton Company (1859) to encourage cotton cultivation elsewhere, including India.
When the American Civil War broke out in 1861, raw cotton imports from America fell to less than three per cent of the normal. By 1862 over 90 per cent of cotton imports into Britain came from India.

In the Bombay Deccan, credit flowed freely: export merchants in Bombay advanced money to urban sahukars, who extended credit to rural moneylenders, who lent to ryots. Ryots expanded cotton cultivation. Rich peasants gained, but most cotton ryots got deeper into debt.

When the Civil War ended in 1865, cotton production in America revived and Indian cotton exports to Britain declined steadily. Export merchants and sahukars were no longer keen to give long-term credit; moneylenders refused loans to ryots.
At the same time, the next revenue settlement increased the demand dramatically, by 50 to 100 per cent. Ryots were squeezed from both sides: no credit and higher revenue.

example.answer: Export merchants → urban sahukars → rural moneylenders → ryots.

topics.title: The experience of injustice: Limitation Law and petitions

learn.hook: A law meant to protect ryots from endless interest ended up trapping them further, because moneylenders made them sign a fresh bond every three years!
points: Ryots were angry when moneylenders refused loans after the cotton boom. They were also angry that moneylenders violated customary norms. One norm was that the interest charged could not be more than the principal; under colonial rule this broke down, and in one case a moneylender charged over ₹2,000 as interest on a loan of ₹100.

In 1859 the British passed a Limitation Law stating that loan bonds signed between moneylenders and ryots would be valid for only three years. The law was meant to check the accumulation of interest over time.

Moneylenders manipulated the law by forcing the ryot to sign a new bond every three years. The unpaid balance, the original loan plus accumulated interest, was entered as the principal of the new bond, and new interest was charged on it.

Ryots' petitions complained that moneylenders refused to give receipts for repayments, entered fictitious figures in bonds, acquired the peasants' harvest at low prices and finally took over their property.
Most ryots were illiterate and did not know what they were signing. Deeds and bonds thus became symbols of a new oppressive system, which explains why, in 1875, ryots burnt them.

example.answer: By renewing bonds every three years with interest added to the principal, so the law that was meant to limit interest actually increased debts.

topics.title: The Deccan Riots Commission and reading official records

learn.hook: An official commission studied the riots and concluded: 'Government revenue is not to blame; the moneylenders are.' Would a government ever blame itself?
points: When the revolt spread in the Deccan, the Bombay government was initially unconcerned. But the Government of India, worried by the memory of 1857, pressured it to set up a commission of enquiry. The commission's report, the Deccan Riots Report, was presented to the British Parliament in 1878.

The commission held enquiries in the districts where the riots had spread, recorded statements of ryots, sahukars and eyewitnesses, compiled statistics on revenue rates, prices and interest rates in different regions, and collated reports from district collectors.

The commission was mainly interested in whether the level of government revenue demand caused the revolt. After examining the evidence, it reported that the government demand was not the cause of peasant anger; it blamed the moneylenders.

This shows the colonial government's reluctance to admit that popular discontent was ever caused by its own actions. Official reports are invaluable sources, but they must be read carefully and juxtaposed with evidence from newspapers, unofficial accounts, legal records and, where possible, oral sources.

Timeline: 1765 Company acquires Diwani of Bengal; 1773 Regulating Act; 1793 Permanent Settlement; around 1800 Santhals come to the Rajmahal hills; 1820s ryotwari in the Bombay Deccan; 1855–56 Santhal hul; 1861 cotton boom begins; 1875 Deccan riots; 1878 Deccan Riots Report.

example.q: Why did the Deccan Riots Commission blame moneylenders rather than revenue demand?
steps: The commission was set up by the colonial government.
Admitting that revenue caused the revolt would blame the government itself.
So it concluded that moneylenders were responsible.
Historians therefore read such reports critically alongside other evidence.
example.answer: Because the colonial government was reluctant to admit its own policies caused discontent; this is why such reports must be read critically.

learn.reallife: Commissions of inquiry are still set up in India after major events; journalists and researchers routinely compare their findings with other evidence.
